page: Microsoft Azure EC8eds_v6 is a memory-optimized virtual machine instance deployed on the Microsoft Hyper-V hypervisor. The instance is powered by dedicated x86_64 Intel processors, supplying 8 dedicated virtual CPUs. Configured with a memory allocation of 64.0 GB, it maintains an 8:1 memory-to-core ratio with 8.0 GB of RAM per vCPU. It does not include hardware graphic accelerators or complimentary public IPv4 addresses.

For scratch space, caching, and temporary data persistence, the EC8eds_v6 includes 472 GB of local NVMe SSD storage directly on the host hardware. The system also supports Azure Premium Storage for persistent managed disks, separating low-latency ephemeral IO operations from persistent block storage.

Because the instance supplies an elevated memory density alongside dedicated compute resources and high-speed local NVMe storage, it targets workloads requiring substantial memory buffers and fast local I/O without the financial footprint of large scale-up tiers. Typical deployments include enterprise in-memory databases, memory-centric caching tiers, data analytics, and memory-intensive enterprise application services.
description: Microsoft Azure EC8eds_v6 is a memory-optimized virtual machine built on Microsoft Hyper-V, delivering 8 dedicated x86_64 Intel vCPUs and 64.0 GB of system memory. Operating at an 8:1 memory-to-core allocation (8.0 GB RAM per vCPU), the instance provides substantial memory headroom for memory-constrained workloads without requiring higher core counts. Hardware resources include a bundled 472 GB local NVMe SSD for fast ephemeral scratch storage, alongside compatibility with Azure Premium Storage for external managed disks. The instance contains no dedicated GPUs or complimentary public IPv4 addresses. With its combination of dedicated processor execution, elevated memory capacity, and low-latency local solid-state storage, the EC8eds_v6 is well suited for in-memory databases, distributed caching layers, relational database servers, and data transformation pipelines.
